text: Puerto Rico (abbreviated PR), officially the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, is a self-governing Caribbean island and archipelago organized as an unincorporated territory of the United States under the designation of commonwealth. Located about 1,000 miles (1,600 km) southeast of Miami, Florida, between the Dominican Republic in the Greater Antilles and the U.S. Virgin Islands in the Lesser Antilles, it includes the main island and smaller islands such as Vieques, Culebra, and Mona. With approximately 3.2 million residents, it is divided into 78 municipalities, the most populous being San Juan, followed by those in the San Juan metropolitan area. Spanish and English are the official languages of the government, though Spanish predominates. The island was first settled by Amerindian peoples, including the Ortoiroid, Saladoid, and Taíno, beginning 2,000 to 4,000 years ago; the Taíno were dominant at the time of Christopher Columbus’s arrival in 1493. Spain claimed the island after Columbus’s arrival and colonized it beginning in 1508, with the Taíno population declining due to diseases, exploitation, and warfare. Puerto Rico remained a Spanish possession for 400 years, serving as a strategically significant but secondary colony within the Spanish Empire. By the late 19th century, a distinct Puerto Rican identity emerged from a fusion of European, African, and Indigenous cultures. In 1898, following the Spanish–American War, Puerto Rico was acquired by the United States. Puerto Ricans have been U.S. citizens since 1917 and can move freely between the island and the mainland, though residents are disenfranchised from federal elections and generally do not pay federal income tax. Puerto Rico sends a nonvoting Resident Commissioner to the U.S. Congress and participates in presidential primaries, but it does not have voting representation in Congress, which oversees it under the Puerto Rico Federal Relations Act of 1950. In 1952, Congress approved a territorial constitution that allowed Puerto Ricans to elect a governor, a senate, and a house of representatives. The political status of Puerto Rico remains a subject of ongoing debate. Beginning in the mid-20th century, the U.S. government and the Puerto Rico Industrial Development Company launched economic development projects, leading to a high-income, developed economy classified by the International Monetary Fund as advanced and high-income, ranking 47th on the Human Development Index. The major economic sectors are manufacturing—especially pharmaceuticals, petrochemicals, and electronics—and services, particularly tourism and hospitality. The island’s name, Puerto Rico, means 'rich port' in Spanish; Puerto Ricans often refer to it as Borinquen, derived from Borikén, the Taíno name meaning 'Land of the Valiant Lord.' The terms boricua, borinqueño, and borincano identify Puerto Rican heritage. The island is also known as La Isla del Encanto, meaning 'the island of enchantment.' Columbus named the island San Juan Bautista and the capital Ciudad de Puerto Rico; over time, the entire island came to be known as Puerto Rico, with San Juan as the main port and capital. The U.S. changed the name to Porto Rico after the Treaty of Paris in 1898, later reverting it to Puerto Rico in 1931 via a joint congressional resolution. The official Spanish name is Estado Libre Asociado de Puerto Rico ("Free Associated State of Puerto Rico"), while the English name is Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, a name suggested by architect Luis Muñoz Marín and adopted in 1952. Some critics argue that "commonwealth" is a euphemism masking Puerto Rico’s status as a U.S. territory, which remains subordinate to the U.S. Constitution in areas like foreign affairs and defense, thus not qualifying as a full-fledged associated state under international or U.S. law. The island’s history began with Ortoiroid settlement before 430 BC, and the Taíno culture dominated at the time of Columbus’s arrival. In 1593, Portuguese soldiers, sent by Philip II, established the first garrison at San Felipe del Morro, some of whom married Puerto Rican women, leading to Portuguese surnames in Puerto Rican families. Puerto Rico served as a key military post in conflicts between Spain and other European powers during the 16th, 17th, and 18th centuries and was a stepping-stone in trans-Atlantic travel. Throughout the 19th century, until the Spanish–American War, Puerto Rico and Cuba were Spain’s last Caribbean colonies; to counter independence movements, Spain revived the Royal Decree of Graces of 1815, offering free land to settlers who pledged loyalty to the Crown and the Catholic Church. In 1898, during the Spanish–American War, Puerto Rico was invaded and became a U.S. possession. The Foraker Act of 1900 established a civil government, ending military rule. A U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Ortega v. Lara (1906) affirmed that the U.S. Constitution applied in Puerto Rico and that local laws not conflicting with it remained valid. The Jones Act of 1917 granted Puerto Ricans U.S. citizenship. In 1952, Puerto Rico’s constitution was approved by Congress and Puerto Rican voters, establishing a self-governing framework. Puerto Rico is one of five territories with limited federal representation, including the Federal District. In 2009, the UN Special Committee on Decolonization urged the U.S. to expedite a process allowing Puerto Ricans to exercise their right to self-determination and independence. In November 2012, a two-question referendum was held; 54% opposed the current territorial status, leading to a second question offering statehood, independence, or free association. 61.16% voted for statehood, 33.34% for free association, and 5.49% for independence. In 2016, President Barack Obama signed H.R. 5278, PROMESA, creating a federal Control Board with significant oversight powers over Puerto Rico’s government, including the authority to override decisions by the legislature, governor, and public authorities, with the president appointing all seven voting members. A 2017 referendum on statehood was held but boycotted by some opponents. In 2017, Puerto Rico suffered back-to-back major hurricanes: Category 5 Hurricane Irma on September 7 and Category 4 Hurricane Maria on September 20, causing widespread damage, including complete power outages, 95% loss of cell service, 43% of wastewater treatment plants damaged, 40,000 landslides, 97% of roads blocked, 28% of health facilities damaged, and over 90% of the population applying for assistance. The debt crisis and hurricanes contributed to a population decline of about half a million in the 21st century, with many relocating to the mainland. In the November 3, 2020, general election, a statehood referendum showed 52% support. In 2022, H.R. 8393 passed the U.S. House but not the Senate, supporting a binding referendum without deciding Puerto Rico’s status. In the November 5, 2024, non-binding referendum, voters chose among statehood, independence, or independence with free association, with statehood winning 59%. Jenniffer González-Colón, a pro-statehood candidate, won the 2024 gubernatorial election with nearly 40% of the vote. Puerto Rico includes the main island and smaller islands such as Vieques, Culebra, Mona, Desecheo, and Caja de Muertos; only Culebra and Vieques are inhabited year-round, while Mona is mostly uninhabited except for Department of Natural Resources employees. Monito, Isla de Cabras, and La Isleta de San Juan are smaller islets, with the latter being the only inhabited one, connected to the main island by bridges. The Commonwealth has an area of 3,515 square miles (9,100 km²), of which 3,459 sq mi (8,960 km²) is land and 56 sq mi (150 km²) is water. It is larger than Delaware and Rhode Island but smaller than Connecticut, with a maximum length of 110 mi (180 km) east to west and a width of 40 mi (64 km) north to south. It is the smallest of the Greater Antilles, 80% the size of Jamaica, over 18% of Hispaniola, and 8% of Cuba. The topography is mostly mountainous, with large flat areas in the north and south; the Cordillera Central runs east to west and contains the highest point, Cerro de Punta at 4,390 feet (1,340 m), and El Yunque at 3,494 feet (1,065 m). Puerto Rico has 17 man-made lakes and over 50 rivers, most originating in the Cordillera Central; northern rivers are longer and have higher flow due to greater rainfall. The island is composed of Cretaceous to Eocene volcanic and plutonic rocks, overlain by Oligocene and younger sedimentary rocks; the oldest rocks, about 190 million years old, are in Sierra Bermeja and may represent oceanic crust from the Pacific. Puerto Rico lies at the boundary between the Caribbean and North American plates, experiencing tectonic stresses that cause earthquakes and tsunamis. The 1918 San Fermín earthquake (magnitude 7.5) off Aguadilla caused extensive damage, 116 deaths, and $4 million in losses, contributing to political activism and the rise of the Puerto Rican Nationalist Party. On January 7, 2020, a magnitude 6.4 earthquake occurred, resulting in over $3.1 billion in economic losses. The Puerto Rico Trench, the deepest in the Atlantic, is located about 71 mi (114 km) north of the island, stretching 170 mi (270 km) and reaching a depth of nearly 27,600 ft (8,400 m) at the Milwaukee Deep. The Mona Canyon, between Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic, has steep walls between 1.25 and 2.17 miles (2.01 and 3.49 km) high. The climate is tropical rainforest, with temperatures averaging near 85°F (29°C) in lowlands and 70°F (21°C) in mountains; easterly trade winds prevail year-round. There is a rainy season from April to November and a dry season from December to March. The Cordillera Central creates a rain shadow, causing significant temperature and rainfall variations over short distances, and influences local wind patterns. Daily temperature changes between dry and wet seasons are about 6°F (3.3°C), primarily due to the warm tropical Atlantic Ocean.

Steep walls in Puerto Rico range in height from 1.25 to 2.17 miles (2.01 to 3.49 km) from bottom to top. The island's climate, classified as tropical rainforest in the Köppen system, features warm to hot temperatures year-round, averaging near 85°F (29°C) in lower elevations and 70°F (21°C) in the mountains, with easterly trade winds prevailing throughout the year. A rainy season runs from April to November, followed by a dry season from December to March. The Cordillera Central mountains create a rain shadow, causing significant temperature and rainfall variations over short distances and influencing local wind speed and direction. Seasonal daily temperature changes in lowlands and coastal areas are minimal, with a year-round shift of about 6°F (3.3°C) between dry and wet seasons, primarily due to the tropical Atlantic Ocean modifying cooler air from the north and northwest. Coastal water temperatures average 75°F (24°C) in February and 85°F (29°C) in August. The highest recorded temperature was 110°F (43°C) at Arecibo, while the lowest was 40°F (4°C) in the mountains at Adjuntas, Aibonito, and Corozal. The average annual precipitation is 66 inches (1,676 mm), and climate change has significantly impacted Puerto Rico’s ecosystems and landscapes. The island experiences the Atlantic hurricane season, with tropical cyclones contributing about a quarter of its annual rainfall, more common during La Niña than El Niño. On average, a tropical storm passes near Puerto Rico every five years and a hurricane every seven years. The only Category 5 hurricane to make landfall in Puerto Rico since 1851 was the Lake Okeechobee Hurricane (San Felipe Segundo) in September 1928. In 2017, the island was hit by Category 5 Hurricane Irma and Category 4 Hurricane Maria, causing widespread damage, especially to the electric grid. Puerto Rico has three terrestrial ecoregions: Puerto Rican moist forests, Puerto Rican dry forests, and Greater Antilles mangroves. It hosts two UNESCO biosphere reserves: Luquillo Biosphere Reserve (El Yunque National Forest) and Guánica Biosphere Reserve. Endemic species include 239 plants, 16 birds, and 39 amphibians/reptiles, with 234 plants, 12 birds, and 33 amphibians/reptiles found on the main island. The coquí, a small frog known for its call, is a symbol of Puerto Rican pride; 13 of its 17 species live in El Yunque National Forest, the only tropical rainforest in the U.S. Forest Service system. El Yunque supports over 240 plant species, 26 of which are endemic, and 50 bird species, including the critically endangered Puerto Rican amazon. The Maricao and Toro Negro state forests, part of the moist forest ecoregion, host endangered species such as the Puerto Rican boa, Puerto Rican sharp-shinned hawk, Puerto Rican broad-winged hawk, and elfin woods warbler. The Northern Karst region contains a remaining rainforest tract, with Río Abajo State Forest focusing on reintroducing the highly endangered Puerto Rican parrot outside the Sierra de Luquillo. The Guánica State Forest and Biosphere Reserve contain over 600 plant and animal species, including 48 endangered and 16 endemic species, representing the best-preserved dry forest in the Caribbean. Other dry forest areas are found in the Caribbean Islands National Wildlife Refuge complex (Cabo Rojo, Desecheo, Culebra, Vieques) and the Caja de Muertos and Mona and Monito Islands Nature Reserves. Endemic species in the dry forest ecoregion include the higo chumbo, Puerto Rican crested toad, and Mona ground iguana, the largest land animal native to Puerto Rico. Puerto Rico has three of the seven year-long bioluminescent bays in the Caribbean: Laguna Grande (Fajardo), La Parguera (Lajas), and Puerto Mosquito (Vieques), inhabited by the dinoflagellate Pyrodinium bahamense, though these ecosystems face threats from tourism, pollution, and hurricanes. Puerto Rico operates under a republican government based on the American model with separation of powers, subject to U.S. jurisdiction and sovereignty. All governmental powers are delegated by the U.S. Congress, with the U.S. president as head of state. As an unincorporated territory, Puerto Rico lacks full constitutional protection. The government has three branches: the executive, led by Governor Jenniffer González-Colón; the legislative, a bicameral Legislative Assembly with a Senate headed by José Luis Dalmau and a House of Representatives headed by Speaker Tatito Hernández; and the judicial branch, led by Chief Justice Maite Oronoz Rodríguez, with judges appointed by the governor with Senate approval. Puerto Rico is represented in the U.S. Congress by a nonvoting delegate, the resident commissioner, currently Pablo Hernández Rivera, who can vote in committees but not in the Committee of the Whole. Elections are governed by the Federal Election Commission and the State Elections Commission of Puerto Rico. Puerto Ricans, including U.S. citizens, cannot vote in U.S. presidential elections but can participate in primaries; those who move to a U.S. state or Washington, D.C. can vote in presidential elections. The island has eight senatorial districts, 40 representative districts, and 78 municipalities, with no first-order administrative divisions recognized by the U.S. government. Municipalities are divided into barrios and each has a mayor and municipal legislature elected every four years. San Juan, founded in 1521, is the oldest municipality, followed by San Germán (1570), Coamo (1579), Arecibo (1614), Aguada (1692), and Ponce (1692); 30 communities were established in the 18th century, 34 in the 19th, and six in the 20th, with Florida founded in 1971. Since 1952, the main political parties are the Popular Democratic Party (PPD), the New Progressive Party (PNP), and the Puerto Rican Independence Party (PIP), with the PPD and PNP each holding about 47% of the vote and the PIP about 5%. After 2007, other parties emerged: the Puerto Ricans for Puerto Rico Party (dissolved in 2008), the Movimiento Unión Soberanista (2012), and the Partido del Pueblo Trabajador (2012), none of which gained more than 1% of the vote. Other non-registered parties include the Puerto Rican Nationalist Party, the Socialist Workers Movement, and the Hostosian National Independence Movement. The political relationship between Puerto Rico and the U.S. remains a subject of debate in Puerto Rico, the U.S. Congress, and the United Nations, with the central question being whether Puerto Rico should remain a U.S. unincorporated territory, become a U.S. state, or achieve independence. Constitutionally, Puerto Rico is subject to the plenary powers of the U.S. Congress under Article IV’s territorial clause, meaning federal laws apply, but residents lack voting representation in Congress and do not have full sovereignty, such as managing external relations. The U.S. Supreme Court has stated that once the Constitution is extended to a territory, its coverage is irrevocable. Puerto Ricans became U.S. citizens in 1917 via the Jones–Shafroth Act, but cannot vote in presidential elections, though they participate in primaries. Only fundamental federal rights apply to Puerto Ricans, with other rights determined by U.S. Supreme Court rulings. Puerto Ricans have a long history of military service and have been included in the U.S. draft since 1917. Despite a common misconception, residents pay U.S. federal taxes, including customs, import/export, commodity, and social security taxes, as well as federal payroll taxes like Social Security and Medicare. Residents also pay Commonwealth income taxes, and due to lower income thresholds and lower per-capita income, more residents pay income taxes to local authorities than under the U.S. IRS code, because the Commonwealth has broader responsibilities than U.S. state and local governments. In 2009, Puerto Rico contributed $3.742 billion to the U.S. Treasury. Residents are eligible for Social Security benefits but are excluded from Supplemental Security Income and receive less Medicaid funding than if it were a state. Medicare providers receive less-than-full reimbursements for services in Puerto Rico, despite full contributions. Puerto Rico’s criminal code authority comes from Congress, not local sovereignty, so crimes are tried only in federal or territorial courts to avoid double jeopardy. In 1992, President George H. W. Bush issued a memorandum directing federal agencies to treat Puerto Rico as a state for administrative purposes, without disrupting federal programs. Many federal agencies, including the FBI, FEMA, TSA, and Social Security Administration, have significant operations in Puerto Rico. Puerto Rico has a Commonwealth judicial system similar to U.S. states, with a U.S. federal district court, and Puerto Ricans have served as judges in federal courts, including Sonia Sotomayor, an associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court. Puerto Ricans frequently hold high-level federal positions, including U.S. ambassadorships. Unlike most U.S. states, Puerto Rico has no counties but 78 municipalities, considered county equivalents for U.S. Census purposes, subdivided into barrios. Each municipality has a mayor and municipal legislature elected every four years under the Autonomous Municipalities Act of 1991. Puerto Rico is subject to the Commerce and Territorial Clause, limiting its international engagement but allowing trade agreements with nations like Colombia and Panama. It has trade promotion offices in Spain, the Dominican Republic, Panama, Colombia, Washington, D.C., New York City, and Florida, and previously in Chile, Costa Rica, and Mexico, all requiring U.S. Department of State approval. Most agreements are permitted under existing U.S. trade laws or treaties. Puerto Rico hosts consulates from 41 countries, mostly in the Americas and Europe, with most in San Juan. The Department of State of Puerto Rico, headed by Secretary of State Larry Seilhamer Rodríguez (New Progressive Party), manages international relations and liaises with consuls. The Puerto Rico Federal Affairs Administration and the Office of the Resident Commissioner handle intergovernmental affairs with U.S. entities. Both entities assist the Department of State in engaging with federal agencies such as the U.S. Department of State and the Agency for International Development. The resident commissioner, currently Jenniffer González-Colón (New Progressive Party and Republican Party), elected in 2016, serves as a legislator in the U.S. House of Representatives, voting on committees but not on final legislation. She received more votes than any other official elected in Puerto Rico that year.

The U.S., local and state governments of the U.S., and public or private entities in the U.S. assist the Department of State of Puerto Rico in engaging with Washington, D.C.-based ambassadors and federal agencies involved in Puerto Rico's foreign affairs, such as the U.S. Department of State and the Agency for International Development. The current secretary of state is Larry Seilhamer Rodríguez from the New Progressive Party, and the current director of the Puerto Rico Federal Affairs Administration is Jennifer M. Stopiran, also from the New Progressive Party and a member of the Republican Party of the U.S. The resident commissioner of Puerto Rico, elected by Puerto Ricans to represent them before the federal government, including the U.S. Congress, sits in the U.S. House of Representatives, serves and votes on congressional committees, and functions as a legislator except being denied a vote on the final disposition of legislation on the House floor. The current resident commissioner is Jenniffer González-Colón, a member of the New Progressive Party and the Republican Party, elected in 2016, who received more votes than any other official elected in Puerto Rico that year. Many Puerto Ricans have served as U.S. ambassadors to various nations and international organizations, such as the Organization of American States, mostly in Latin America; for example, Maricarmen Aponte, now an acting assistant secretary of state, previously served as U.S. ambassador to El Salvador. As an unincorporated U.S. territory, Puerto Rico's defense is provided by the U.S. under the Treaty of Paris, with the president of the U.S. as commander-in-chief. Puerto Rico has its own National Guard and a state defense force, the Puerto Rico State Guard, which by local law is under the authority of the Puerto Rico National Guard. The commander-in-chief of both local forces is the governor of Puerto Rico, who delegates authority to the Puerto Rico adjutant general, currently Major General José J. Reyes; the Adjutant General delegates authority over the State Guard to another officer but retains authority over the Puerto Rico National Guard as a whole. U.S. military installations in Puerto Rico were part of the U.S. Atlantic Command (LANTCOM after 1993 USACOM), which had authority over all U.S. military operations in the Atlantic, until 1999 when U.S. Atlantic Command was renamed and given a new mission as U.S. Joint Forces Command, after which Puerto Rico fell under the responsibility of U.S. Northern Command. Formerly, the Naval Forces Caribbean (NFC) and the Fleet Air Caribbean (FAIR) were based at the Roosevelt Roads Naval Station, with NFC overseeing all U.S. naval activity in the Caribbean and FAIR overseeing all U.S. military flights and air operations over the Caribbean. With the closure of Roosevelt Roads and Vieques Island training facilities, the U.S. Navy has largely exited Puerto Rico, except for ships that pass through, and the only significant military presence is the U.S. Army at Fort Buchanan, the Puerto Rican Army and Air National Guards, and the U.S. Coast Guard. Protests over noise from bombing practice led to the closure of the naval base, resulting in a loss of 6,000 jobs and an annual decrease in local income of $300 million. A branch of the U.S. Army National Guard is stationed in Puerto Rico—the Puerto Rico Army National Guard—performing missions equivalent to those of other U.S. state Army National Guards, including ground defense, disaster relief, and civil unrest control. The local National Guard also includes the Puerto Rico Air National Guard, which performs missions equivalent to those of U.S. state Air National Guards. Throughout the 20th century, the U.S. had about 25 military or naval installations in Puerto Rico, with the largest being the former Roosevelt Roads Naval Station in Ceiba, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Training Facility (AFWTF) on Vieques, the National Guard training facility at Camp Santiago in Salinas, Fort Allen in Juana Diaz, Fort Buchanan in San Juan, the former U.S. Air Force's Ramey Air Force Base in Aguadilla, and the Puerto Rico Air National Guard's Muñiz Air National Guard Base in San Juan. The former U.S. Navy facilities at Roosevelt Roads, Vieques, and Sabana Seca have been deactivated and partially turned over to the local government. Aside from U.S. Coast Guard and Puerto Rico National Guard facilities, only two military installations remain in Puerto Rico: the U.S. Army's small Fort Buchanan (supporting local veterans and reserve units) and the Puerto Rico Air National Guard's Muñiz Air Base (the C-130 Fleet). In recent years, the U.S. Congress has considered deactivating these installations, but they have been opposed by diverse public and private entities in Puerto Rico, including retired military personnel who rely on Fort Buchanan for services. Puerto Ricans have participated in many U.S. military conflicts, including the American Revolution, when volunteers from Puerto Rico, Cuba, and Mexico fought the British in 1779 under General Bernardo de Gálvez (1746–1786), and continue to be disproportionately represented in present-day conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan. The most notable example is the 65th Infantry Regiment of the U.S. Army, nicknamed The Borinqueneers, from the original Taíno name of the island (Borinquen), which participated in World War I, World War II, the Korean War, and the war on terror, and was awarded the Congressional Gold Medal in 2014 for heroism during the Korean War. A significant number of Puerto Ricans serve in the U.S. Armed Forces, primarily as National Guard members and civilian employees; the overall military-related community is estimated at 100,000, including retired personnel. Fort Buchanan has about 4,000 military and civilian personnel, and approximately 17,000 people are members of the Puerto Rico Army and Air National Guards or U.S. Reserve forces. The insular legal system in Puerto Rico is a blend of civil law and common law. Puerto Rico is the only current U.S. jurisdiction whose legal system operates primarily in a language other than American English—namely, Spanish. Because the U.S. federal government operates primarily in English, all Puerto Rican attorneys must be bilingual to litigate in English in U.S. federal courts and to litigate federal preemption issues in Puerto Rican courts. Title 48 of the United States Code outlines the role of the U.S. Code for U.S. territories and insular areas such as Puerto Rico. After the U.S. government assumed control in 1901, it initiated legal reforms adopting codes of criminal law, criminal procedure, and civil procedure modeled after those in California. Although Puerto Rico has since transitioned criminal and civil procedure from statutory law to rules promulgated by the judiciary, several portions of its criminal law still reflect the influence of the California Penal Code. The judicial branch is headed by the chief justice of the Puerto Rico Supreme Court, the only appellate court required by the Constitution; all other courts are created by the Legislative Assembly of Puerto Rico. There is also a Federal District Court for Puerto Rico, and someone accused of a criminal act at the federal level may not be accused for the same act in a Commonwealth court, and vice versa, because Puerto Rico, as an unincorporated territory, lacks sovereignty separate from Congress as a state does. The U.S. Supreme Court held in 2016 that such a parallel accusation would constitute double jeopardy. The homicide rate of 19.2 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2014 was significantly higher than any U.S. state, with about 80% of homicides being drug-related, and most victims being gang members or drug traffickers. In 1992, the FBI made armed carjacking a federal crime and rates decreased according to statistics, but as of 2019, the problem persisted in municipalities like Guaynabo, with thirty carjackings reported between January 1, 2019, and March 14, 2019. Puerto Rico is classified as a high-income economy by the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, considered the most competitive economy in Latin America by the World Economic Forum, and ranks highly on the Human Development Index. According to the World Bank, gross national income per capita in Puerto Rico in 2020 was $21,740. The economy is mainly driven by manufacturing (primarily pharmaceuticals, textiles, petrochemicals, and electronics) and services (primarily finance, insurance, real estate, and tourism), with agriculture representing less than 1% of GNP. In recent years, it has become a popular destination for MICE (meetings, incentives, conferencing, exhibitions), with a modern convention center district overlooking the Port of San Juan. Responsibility for San Juan port inspections lies with the Puerto Rico Port Authority (PPQ). Between 1984 and 2000, the San Juan PPQ station recorded 7.74% of all interceptions, ranking fourth in the country, second for insects, and third for pathogens. Most species intercepted are originally from South America or elsewhere in the Caribbean due to Puerto Rico's position as an intermediary on the way to the mainland, making it one of the worst locations for cut flowers and other plant parts in terms of both number of problems and diversity of species for insects and pathogens in baggage and cargo. Pathogen interceptions increased by 17% from 1999–2000 compared to 1985–1986. Puerto Rico's geography and political status are key factors in its economic prosperity, primarily due to its small size, lack of natural resources, dependence on imports, and vulnerability to U.S. foreign policy and trading restrictions, especially in its shipping industry. Puerto Rico experienced a recession from 2006 to 2011, interrupted by four quarters of growth, and entered another recession in 2013 following growing fiscal imbalance and the expiration of IRS Section 936 corporate incentives, which had provided tax exemptions for U.S. corporations settling in Puerto Rico and allowed their insular subsidiaries to send earnings to parent corporations without paying federal taxes. Puerto Rico has maintained relatively low inflation and a purchasing power parity per capita higher than 80% of the world. By American standards, Puerto Rico is underdeveloped, poorer than Mississippi, the poorest U.S. state, with 41% of its population below the poverty line, yet it has the highest GDP per capita in Latin America. Its main trading partners are the United States, Ireland, and Japan, with most products coming from East Asia, mainly China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan. Puerto Rico's dependency on oil for transportation and electricity generation, as well as on food imports and raw materials, makes it volatile and highly reactive to global economic and climate changes. Tourism is also a significant part of the economy; in 2017, Hurricane Maria caused severe damage to the island and its infrastructure, estimated at $100 billion, disrupting tourism for months. By April 2019, only a few hotels were closed, and life for tourists in and around the capital had largely returned to normal. By October 2019, nearly all popular tourist amenities in major destinations such as San Juan, Ponce, and Arecibo were operational, and tourism was rebounding, which was vital for the economy since tourism provides up to 10% of Puerto Rico's GDP according to Discover Puerto Rico. A tourism campaign launched by Discover Puerto Rico in 2018 aimed to highlight the island's culture and history, branding it distinct from other Caribbean destinations, with plans to continue in 2019. In early 2017, the Puerto Rican government-debt crisis posed serious problems, with outstanding bond debt reaching $70 billion. The Commonwealth had been defaulting on many debts, including bonds, since 2015. With debt payments due, the governor faced the risk of a government shutdown and failure to fund the managed health care system. A letter sent to Congress by the Secretary of the Treasury and the Secretary of Health and Human Services warned that without action before April, Puerto Rico's ability to execute contracts for Fiscal Year 2018 with its managed care organizations would be threatened, putting at risk the health care of up to 900,000 impoverished U.S. citizens living in Puerto Rico, and urged Congress to enact measures recommended by both Republicans and Democrats to fix Puerto Rico's inequitable health care financing structure and promote sustained economic growth. Initially, the oversight board created under PROMESA required Puerto Rico's governor Ricardo Rosselló to deliver a fiscal turnaround plan by January 28. Just before that deadline, the control board extended the deadline to February 28 to present a fiscal plan, including negotiations with creditors for debt restructuring, and extended a moratorium on lawsuits by debtors to May 31. It is essential for Puerto Rico to reach restructuring deals to avoid a bankruptcy-like process under PROMESA. An internal survey by the Puerto Rican Economists Association revealed that the majority of Puerto Rican economists reject the policy recommendations of the Board and the Rosselló government, with more than 80% arguing in favor of auditing the debt. In early August 2017, the financial oversight board planned to institute two days off without pay per month for government employees, down from the original plan of four days per month, which was expected to save $218 million; Governor Rosselló rejected the plan as unjustified and unnecessary. Pension reforms were also discussed, including a proposal for a 10% reduction in benefits to address $50 billion in unfunded pension liabilities. Puerto Rico has an operating budget of about $9.8 billion with expenses at about $10.4 billion, creating a structural deficit of $775 million (about 7.9% of the budget). The practice of approving budgets with a structural deficit has continued for 26 consecutive years starting in 2000, with all budgets in those years, including present time, contemplating issuing bonds to cover projected deficits rather than making structural adjustments. This practice has increased Puerto Rico's cumulative debt, as the government had been issuing bonds to balance its actual budget since 1973. Projected deficits added substantial burdens to an already indebted nation that had accrued a public debt of $71 billion or about 70% of Puerto Rico's gross domestic product. This triggered an ongoing government-debt crisis after Puerto Rico's general obligation bonds were downgraded to speculative non-investment grade ("junk status") by three credit-rating agencies. In terms of financial control, about 9.6%—or $1.5 billion—of Puerto Rico's central government budget expenses for FY2014 were expected to be spent on debt service. Harsher budget cuts are expected as Puerto Rico must repay larger chunks of debt in the coming years. For practical reasons, the budget is divided into two aspects: a "general budget" funded exclusively by the Department of Treasury of Puerto Rico, and a "consolidated budget" funded by the general budget, government-owned corporations, expected loan revenue, bond sales, federal subsidies, and other funds. The consolidated budget is usually three times the size of the general budget; currently $29 billion and $9.0 billion respectively. Almost one out of every four dollars in the consolidated budget comes from U.S. federal subsidies, and government-owned corporations compose more than 31% of the consolidated budget. The critical aspect is bond sales, which comprise 7% of the consolidated budget—a ratio that has increased annually due to the government's inability to prepare a balanced budget and generate sufficient income to cover all expenses. The budget is divided into two components: a "general budget" funded solely by the Department of Treasury of Puerto Rico, and a "consolidated budget" that includes funding from the general budget, government-owned corporations, expected loan revenue, government bond sales, U.S. federal subsidies, and other sources. The consolidated budget is typically three times larger than the general budget, currently standing at $29 billion and $9.0 billion, respectively. Approximately one in every four dollars in the consolidated budget comes from U.S. federal subsidies, and government-owned corporations account for more than 31% of it. Bond sales make up 7% of the consolidated budget, a figure that has increased annually due to the government’s inability to balance its budget or generate sufficient income to cover expenses. These corporations, such as the Puerto Rico Highways and Transportation Authority (PRHTA), the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority (PREPA), and the Puerto Rico Aqueducts and Sewers Authority (PRASA), are not self-sufficient and have contributed significantly to public debt. For instance, in FY2011, these corporations reported combined losses exceeding $1.3 billion, with PRHTA losing $409 million, PREPA losing $272 million, and PRASA losing $112 million. These losses have been offset by bond issuance, which now accounts for more than 40% of Puerto Rico’s total public debt. From FY2000 to FY2010, Puerto Rico’s debt grew at a compound annual growth rate of 9% while GDP remained stagnant. In early July 2017, PREPA effectively became bankrupt after defaulting on a $9 billion bond restructuring plan and planned to seek court protection. The cost of living in Puerto Rico is high and has risen over the past decade, partly due to the Jones Act of 1920, which prohibits foreign-flagged ships from carrying cargo between U.S. ports, forcing goods to be transported via U.S.-flagged vessels and increasing shipping costs. Although the Government Accountability Office in 2013 suggested that repealing or amending the Jones Act could reduce shipping costs, it concluded the effects on Puerto Rico and the U.S. were highly uncertain, particularly for the shipping industry and military readiness. A 2018 study by Reeve & Associates and Estudios Tecnicos found the Jones Act has no impact on retail prices or the cost of living. Puerto Rico’s transportation system includes roads maintained by the Highways and Transportation Authority, public buses and the Tren Urbano metro in San Juan, seaborne ferries, and carros públicos. The island has three international airports—Luis Muñoz Marín in Carolina, Mercedita in Ponce, and Rafael Hernández in Aguadilla—with the former being the largest in the Caribbean, and 27 local airports. There are nine ports, with San Juan Port being the largest and busiest in the Caribbean and the 10th busiest in the U.S. by cargo volume, and the Port of the Americas in Ponce undergoing expansion to reach 1.5 million twenty-foot equivalent units annually. PREPA, the government-owned entity responsible for electricity generation, transmission, and distribution, was a monopoly until 2018. On July 20, 2018, Law 120-2018 was signed, allowing PREPA to sell infrastructure and services; a contract signed on June 22, 2020, transferred operations to LUMA Energy, effective June 1, 2021, marking a partial privatization of the power grid, which sparked protests and uncertainty among the public and former workers. PRASA, the government-owned water authority, is the sole provider of water services and is designated by Law No. 40 of May 1, 1945. Telecommunications in Puerto Rico include radio, television, fixed and mobile phones, and the internet, regulated by the U.S. Federal Communications Commission. As of 2007, there were 30 TV stations, 125 radio stations, and about 1 million TV sets. Puerto Rico has unique amateur radio prefixes, such as KP4, KP3, NP3, NP4, WP3, WP4, and KP5/NP5/WP5, used across the archipelago, and amateur radio operators often display their call signs on special vehicle plates and have played a key role in disaster relief. The population of Puerto Rico reflects influences from indigenous settlement, European colonization, slavery, migration, and its status as a U.S. unincorporated territory. According to the 2020 U.S. census, Puerto Rico had 3,285,874 residents, an 11.8% decline since 2010, with a peak of 3,808,610 in 2000 and a drop to 3,725,789 in 2010. The most populous municipality is San Juan, with 342,259 residents in 2020, and eight of the ten most populous cities are within San Juan’s metropolitan area. As of 2020, 98.9% of the population identified as Hispanic or Latino, of whom 95.5% were Puerto Rican and 3.4% were of non-Puerto Rican Hispanic origin, while only 1.1% were non-Hispanic. Just 17.1% identified as White, a drop of nearly 80% from earlier, and 49.8% identified as multiracial—up from 3% in 2010—while 25.5% selected "some other race alone." Historical censuses were conducted by Spain in 1765, 1775, 1800, 1815, 1832, 1846, and 1857, with some data untabulated. In 1858, the population was 341,015 free colored, 300,430 white, and 41,736 enslaved; by 1887, the population was around 800,000, with 320,000 black. During the 19th century, immigration came primarily from Spain, including the Canary Islands and Andalusia, and later from other Spanish regions and non-Hispanic countries such as France, Lebanon, Portugal, Ireland, Scotland, Germany, and Italy, under the Real Cédula de Gracias de 1815. Between 1960 and 1990, Puerto Rico’s census did not ask about race or ethnicity; the 2000 census introduced a racial self-identification question, with most identifying as white and Latino. A 2003 University of Puerto Rico study of 800 individuals found 61.1% had Indigenous mitochondrial DNA, 26.4% had African markers, and 12.5% had European descent, leading to a resurgence of Taíno identity, with 19,839 identifying as "American Indian or Alaskan Native" in 2010—up 49% from 2000. Most recent immigrants come from Latin America, with over half from the Dominican Republic (53% of non-Puerto Rican Hispanics, or about 1.8% of the population), and others from Cuba, Colombia, Mexico, Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Panama, Ecuador, Spain, and Jamaica. Non-Puerto Rican U.S. citizens, mostly White Americans and a smaller number of Black Americans, also settle in Puerto Rico, with a small number from the U.S. Virgin Islands. Nuyoricans and other mainland Puerto Ricans engage in circular migration. Emigration began after World War II due to poverty, cheap airfares, and government promotion, continuing despite economic improvements and declining birth rates. Population decline accelerated after hurricanes Maria and Irma in 2017, due to economic hardship and natural disasters. According to the 2020 census, the number of Puerto Ricans living outside the island in the U.S. is nearly double those living in Puerto Rico, and because those who leave are often better educated, this exacerbates economic strain. As of July 1, 2019, the population had declined by 532,095 since 2010. The population of Puerto Rico, estimated by the U.S. Census Bureau at 3.4 million, had declined by 532,095 people since the 2010 Census. The official languages of the executive branch of government are Spanish and English, with the Puerto Rican legislature declaring Spanish as the first and English as the second official language in 2015. Spanish remains the sole official language of the Commonwealth judiciary, despite a 1902 English-only language law, though all official business of the U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico is conducted in English. English is spoken as a primary language by less than 10% of the population, while Spanish is the dominant language in business, education, and daily life, spoken by nearly 95% of residents. Among people aged five and older, 94.3% speak only Spanish at home, 5.5% speak English, and 0.2% speak other languages. A 2012 Pew Research survey reported an adult literacy rate of 90.4% based on United Nations data, and as of 2002, the overall literacy rate was 94.1%, with 93.9% for males and 94.4% for females. Public school instruction is conducted almost entirely in Spanish, with about a dozen of the over 1,400 public schools running pilot English-only programs, often facing objections from staff due to limited English fluency. English is taught as a compulsory second language from elementary to high school. The deaf community uses American Sign Language and Puerto Rican Sign Language. Puerto Rican Spanish has evolved with unique vocabulary and syntax, incorporating Taíno and English words, with the largest influence from the Canary Islands; Taíno loanwords are common in vegetation, natural phenomena, and native instruments, while West African-derived words appear in food, music, and dance, especially in coastal areas with African-descended populations. Christianity is the dominant religion, with Catholicism introduced by Spanish colonists and established through the first dioceses authorized by Pope Julius II in 1511, and priests established in 1512, with one priest per church by 1759. Pope John Paul II visited Puerto Rico in October 1984, and all municipalities have at least one Catholic church, typically located in the town center. Protestantism, suppressed under Spanish rule, reemerged under U.S. governance, making Puerto Rico more interconfessional, though Catholicism remains dominant. The first Protestant church, Iglesia de la Santísima Trinidad, was founded in Ponce in 1872 by the Anglican Diocese of Antigua and was the first non-Catholic church in the Spanish Empire in the Americas. Sources vary on religious demographics: Pablo Ramos (1998) reported 38% Catholic, 28% Pentecostal, and 18% independent churches, with Protestants totaling nearly 46% of the population; another researcher in 1997 estimated 33–38% Protestant, mostly Pentecostal, and projected 75% evangelical by 2022. A 2014 Pew Research report found 56% Catholic, 33% Protestant, and 8% unaffiliated, with Protestants largely Pentecostal and other religions at 2%, while atheists made up 1%; a prior survey of Puerto Ricans in the mainland U.S. found 45% Catholic, 29% Protestant, and 20% unaffiliated. An Associated Press article in March 2014 stated over 70% identified as Catholic. There is a small Eastern Orthodox community, centered in San German and Carolina with services in English and Spanish, a Syriac Orthodox church in Aguada, and an Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church in Utuado, representing the only Oriental Orthodox denominations; a Greek Catholic Church exists in Trujillo Alto, and Orthodox Christians accounted for 1% of the population in 2010. In 2017, the first Eastern Catholic Church was established. In 2023, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints dedicated a temple in San Juan and reported approximately 23,000 members. In 2015, 25,832 Jehovah's Witnesses represented about 0.70% of the population with 324 congregations. Puerto Rico has the largest Jewish community in the Caribbean, at roughly 3,000, and is the only Caribbean island with all three Jewish movements—Conservative, Reform, and Orthodox—represented; the first synagogue, Sha'are Zedeck, was established in 1952 by American Jews. In 2007, there were about 5,000 Muslims, or 0.13% of the population, with eight mosques, mostly in Río Piedras and Caguas, and most of Palestinian or Jordanian descent; there is also a Baháʼí community. Buddhism is represented by Nichiren, Zen, and Tibetan traditions, with a branch of the New York Padmasambhava Buddhist Center in San Juan; there are also atheist activist groups and the Pastafarian Church of Puerto Rico, and an ISKCON temple in Gurabo dedicated to Krishna with two preaching centers in the San Juan area. Taíno religious practices have been revived by a few advocates, and African religious traditions, including Santería (Yoruba) and Palo Mayombe (Kongo), persist, often syncretized with Christianity. In 1940, Juanita García Peraza founded the Mita Congregation, the first religion of Puerto Rican origin. The first school in Puerto Rico was the Escuela de Gramática, established in 1513 by Bishop Alonso Manso in the area where the Cathedral of San Juan was built, offering free instruction in Latin, literature, history, science, art, philosophy, and theology. Education in Puerto Rico is divided into primary (grades 1–6), secondary (grades 7–12), and higher levels (undergraduate and graduate studies). As of 2000, 60.0% of the population had a high school degree or higher, and 18.3% had a bachelor’s degree or higher. Primary education is compulsory from ages 5 to 18. As of 2010, there were 1539 public and 806 private schools. The largest university system is the public University of Puerto Rico (UPR) with 11 campuses; major private systems include Sistema Universitario Ana G. Mendez (Universidad del Turabo, Metropolitan University, Universidad del Este), Inter American University, Pontifical Catholic University, Universidad Politécnica de Puerto Rico, and Universidad del Sagrado Corazón. Puerto Rico has four medical schools and three ABA-approved law schools. In 2017, there were 69 hospitals; average life expectancy in 2021 was 82.1 years, up from 78.7 years in 2010. The Reforma de Salud de Puerto Rico (La Reforma) provides healthcare to the poor and indigent through private insurance contracts, administered by the Puerto Rico Health Insurance Administration. Puerto Rican culture is a blend of European (Spanish, Italian, French, German, Irish), African, and recent North and South American influences, with many Cubans and Dominicans relocating in recent decades. Spanish contributed the language, Catholicism, and cultural values, while the U.S. introduced English, the university system, and some holidays. The University of Puerto Rico was officially founded on March 12, 1903, from the earlier "Escuela Normal Industrial" established in Fajardo in 1899. Music is central to Puerto Rican culture, shaped by Spanish and African traditions and influenced by Caribbean and North American movements. Puerto Rico has many symbols, with only the Flor de Maga officially recognized by the government; other traditional symbols include the Puerto Rican spindalis, kapok tree, coquí frog, jíbaro, Taíno Indian, and Cerro Las Tetas. Architecture reflects centuries of Spanish and American influence, including Spanish colonial, Ibero-Islamic, art deco, and post-modern styles, with regional variations. Old San Juan, along with Santurce, was a municipality from 1864 to 1951, and is known for its shops, historic sites, museums, cafés, homes, plazas, and churches such as San José Church and the Cathedral of San Juan Bautista, which contains the tomb of Juan Ponce de León and houses the oldest Catholic elementary school, Colegio de Párvulos, built in 1865. The old district is partially enclosed by massive walls, with notable forts like Fort San Felipe del Morro, Fort San Cristóbal, and La Fortaleza (also the governor’s executive mansion) serving as key defenses and part of the San Juan National Historic Site. In the 1940s, parts of Old San Juan fell into disrepair, leading to numerous renovation efforts, including a successful effort to preserve the Carmelite Convent by converting it into Hotel El Convento. This model of restoration has influenced cities like Havana, Lima, and Cartagena. Ponce Creole is a unique architectural style developed between 1895 and 1920 in Ponce, blending French, Spanish, and Caribbean vernacular elements to suit the region’s climate and coastal environment, using wood and masonry with features from Classical revival, Spanish Revival, and Victorian styles. Puerto Rican art includes santos—religious sculptures made from native wood, clay, and stone, painted in vivid colors, traditionally placed on household altars as messengers between earth and heaven—and caretas, masks with horns and fangs used in carnivals, derived from Spanish and African traditions, often made of papier-mâché, coconut shells, or metal screening, originally in red and black but now in varied bright colors. Puerto Rican literature evolved from oral storytelling; Spanish colonial authorities prohibited native writing, allowing only Crown-commissioned works, such as Diego de Torres Vargas’s 1647 Descripción de la Ciudad e Isla de Puerto Rico, the first detailed geographic account of the island. Early writers like Manuel A. Alonso, author of El Gíbaro (1849), and Eugenio María de Hostos, who wrote La peregrinación de Bayoán (1863) and later focused on essays for social change, laid foundations. In the late 19th century, with the arrival of printing presses and the Royal Academy of Belles Letters, literature flourished, with Alejandro Tapia y Rivera (the "Father of Puerto Rican Literature") publishing The Historical Library of Puerto Rico and Cayetano Coll y Toste producing The Indo-Antillano Vocabulary. Manuel Zeno Gandía wrote La Charca (1894) on mountainous coffee region life, and Antonio S. Pedreira described cultural survival in Insularismo after the American invasion. The Nuyorican Movement, influenced by the 1940s diaspora, significantly shaped Puerto Rican literature, leading to a flourishing of authors, journalists, poets, novelists, playwrights, essayists, and screenwriters whose influence extends beyond the island.

The founding of the Royal Academy of Belles Letters marked the beginning of a flourishing of Puerto Rican literature. Early writers who expressed political views against Spanish colonial rule were journalists. Alejandro Tapia y Rivera, known as the Father of Puerto Rican Literature, introduced a new era in historiography with the publication of The Historical Library of Puerto Rico. Cayetano Coll y Toste, another prominent Puerto Rican historian and writer, contributed The Indo-Antillano Vocabulary, which provides insight into Taíno life. Manuel Zeno Gandía published La Charca in 1894, detailing the difficult conditions in remote, mountainous coffee regions. Antonio S. Pedreira, in his work Insularismo, explored the cultural survival of Puerto Rican identity after the American invasion. During the Puerto Rican diaspora of the 1940s, the Nuyorican Movement significantly influenced Puerto Rican literature, which continued to thrive, producing notable authors, journalists, poets, novelists, playwrights, essayists, and screenwriters. This literary influence has extended beyond the island to the United States and globally. Over the past fifty years, key figures include Ed Vega (Omaha Bigelow), Miguel Piñero (Short Eyes), Piri Thomas (Down These Mean Streets), Giannina Braschi (Yo-Yo Boing!), Rosario Ferrer (Eccentric Neighborhoods), and Esmeralda Santiago (When I Was Puerto Rican). The mass media in Puerto Rico includes local radio, television, and newspapers, most of which are in Spanish, along with three U.S. Armed Forces Radio and Television Service stations. Daily newspapers include El Nuevo Día, El Vocero, Índice, Metro, and Primera Hora; El Vocero, Índice, and Metro are distributed free of charge. Weekly or regional publications include Claridad, La Perla del Sur, La Opinión, Visión, and La Estrella del Norte. Local television channels such as WIPR-TV, Telemundo, WLII-DT (Teleonce), WAPA-TV, and WKAQ-TV offer local content. Puerto Rican music has evolved from diverse cultural roots, primarily Spain and West Africa, with influences from other parts of Europe, the Caribbean, and the United States. Today, it includes Indigenous genres like bomba, plena, aguinaldo, danza, and popular salsa, as well as modern hybrids such as reggaeton and Latin trap, widely popularized by Bad Bunny. The cuatro, a national instrument made by the "Jibaro" people of the mountains, originally had four steel strings but now has five double steel strings; when held upright from right to left, the strings are G, D, A, E, B. In classical music, Puerto Rico hosts the Orquesta Sinfónica de Puerto Rico and the Orquesta Filarmónica de Puerto Rico, with the annual Casals Festival in San Juan attracting international classical musicians. The legendary tenor Antonio Paoli was so renowned that he performed private recitals for Pope Pius X and Tsar Nicholas II of Russia; in 1907, he became the first operatic artist in history to record an entire opera, performing Pagliacci by Ruggiero Leoncavallo in Milan, Italy. International musical success has been achieved by artists such as Menudo, Ricky Martin, and Bad Bunny. Puerto Rico has been featured on four U.S. postal stamps: one in 1937 honoring Insular Territories, featuring 'La Fortaleza'; a 3-cent stamp on April 27, 1949, commemorating the first free election for governor, which marked the inauguration of Luis Muñoz Marín, the first democratically elected governor; an 8-cent stamp issued on September 12, 1971, celebrating San Juan’s 450th anniversary with a sentry box from Castillo San Felipe del Morro; and in the "Flags of our nation" series (2008–2012), five territorial flags were included, with a 2011 forever stamp featuring the Puerto Rico flag illustrated by a bird. Puerto Rican cuisine stems from European (Spanish), African, and Native Taíno traditions, using ingredients such as grains, legumes, herbs, starchy tubers, vegetables, meat, poultry, seafood, and fruits. Main dishes include mofongo, arroz con gandules, pasteles, and pig roast (lechón); beverages include maví and piña colada; desserts include flan, arroz con dulce, piraguas, brazo gitanos, tembleque, polvorones, and dulce de leche. Baseball became one of the first widely popular sports in Puerto Rico, with the Puerto Rico Baseball League serving as the only active professional winter league. No Major League Baseball franchise or affiliate plays in Puerto Rico, though San Juan hosted the Montreal Expos in 2003 and 2004 before they moved to Washington, D.C. and became the Nationals. The Puerto Rico national baseball team has won one gold, four silver, and four bronze medals in the World Cup of Baseball, won fourteen Caribbean Series titles, and participated in the World Baseball Classic. In March 2006, Hiram Bithorn Stadium in San Juan hosted the opening and second rounds of the World Baseball Classic. Hall of Famers Roberto Clemente (1973), Orlando Cepeda (1999), and Roberto Alomar (2011) are Puerto Rican players. Boxing, basketball, and volleyball are also popular sports. Wilfredo Gómez and McWilliams Arroyo won their divisions at the World Amateur Boxing Championships; José Pedraza earned a silver medal, and three boxers—José Luis Vellón, Nelson Dieppa, and McJoe Arroyo—finished third. Puerto Rico ranks third in the number of boxing world champions and leads globally in champions per capita, with notable champions including Miguel Cotto, Félix Trinidad, Wilfred Benítez, and Gómez. The Puerto Rico national basketball team joined the International Basketball Federation in 1957 and has won over 30 international medals, including gold in three FIBA Americas Championships. On August 8, 2004, during the 2004 Summer Olympics in Athens, Greece, the team made history by becoming the first to defeat the United States in an Olympic tournament since the integration of NBA players, winning 92–73 in their inaugural game. Baloncesto Superior Nacional is the top professional basketball league, established in 1930. Puerto Rico is a member of FIFA and CONCACAF, and in 2008, the Puerto Rico Soccer League was founded as the first unified league. Other sports include professional wrestling and road running; the World Wrestling Council and International Wrestling Association are the largest promotions on the main island. The World's Best 10K, held annually in San Juan, is among the world’s top 20 competitive races. The "Puerto Rico All Stars" team has won twelve world championships in unicycle basketball. Organized streetball has gained attention, with teams like "Puerto Rico Street Ball" competing against organizations such as the Capitanes de Arecibo and AND1's Mixtape Tour Team; after an initial visit, AND1 returned in 2013 as part of their Live Tour, losing to the Puerto Rico Streetballers. Practitioners have earned international recognition, including Orlando "El Gato" Meléndez, the first Puerto Rican-born athlete to play for the Harlem Globetrotters. Puerto Rico participates in all international competitions, including the Summer and Winter Olympics, the Pan American Games, the Caribbean World Series, and the Central American and Caribbean Games. It hosted the Pan Am Games in 1979 (officially in San Juan), the Central American and Caribbean Games in 1993 (Ponce) and 2010 (Mayagüez). Puerto Rican athletes have won ten Olympic medals (two gold, two silver, six bronze), with the first in 1948 by boxer Juan Evangelista Venegas; Monica Puig won Puerto Rico’s first Olympic gold in women’s tennis singles at the Rio 2016 Games. The geographic coordinates of the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico are 18°12′N 66°30′W (18.2°N 66.5°W).
